business_problem: Nestle needs to identify new packaging materials that meet product-specific functional requirements while preserving food safety and quality, but the research process is meticulous and can take years.
solution_summary: Nestle R&D worked with IBM Research to build a generative AI system for sustainable packaging discovery. The implementation starts with ingesting material knowledge from public and proprietary documents, which the team used to construct a knowledge base of known packaging materials. That curated corpus was then used to fine-tune a fit-for-purpose chemical language model so it could learn molecular structure representations relevant to barrier-material design. On top of that learned representation, the teams applied IBM Research's regression transformer to model correlations between structural molecular features and physical-chemical properties. The resulting model serves packaging researchers by proposing entirely new high-barrier materials that can protect sensitive products from moisture, temperature swings, and oxygen, helping Nestle evaluate future options against cost, recyclability, and functional packaging requirements.

data_flow: Public and proprietary documents are ingested to build a knowledge base of known materials, which is curated into a corpus for fine-tuning a chemical language model. Its learned molecular representations are used with a regression transformer that predicts structure-property relationships and proposes new high-barrier packaging materials for Nestle researchers to assess for cost, recyclability, and functional fit.
business_outcome: Nestle will use the model to identify future high-barrier packaging materials while considering cost, recyclability, and functionality, with the stated aim of optimizing development of more sustainable packaging solutions.
